title: Separated Configuration
content: A `SepConfig d n` packages $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a proof that all pairwise distances are at least 1. This is the fundamental abstraction: unit-distance problems ask how many pairs can achieve the minimum allowed distance.
mathContext: $C = (p_1, \ldots, p_n) \in (\mathbb{R}^d)^n$ with $\|p_i - p_j\| \ge 1$ for all $i \ne j$.

title: Unit-Distance Pair Count
content: Counts ordered pairs $(i,j)$ with $i < j$ and $\|p_i - p_j\| = 1$. The ordering constraint $i < j$ avoids double-counting. This is the extremal quantity $f_d(n)$ that Erdős asked to determine.

title: Unit-Distance Degree
content: The number of points at distance exactly 1 from a given point $p_i$. Bounded above by the kissing number $\tau(d)$, since all such neighbors lie on the unit sphere around $p_i$ with mutual distance $\ge 1$.

title: 1D Separated Configuration
content: Specialized 1D structure using real-valued points and absolute value distance. The 1D case is treated separately because it admits a complete, machine-verified solution: $f_1(n) = n-1$ exactly.

title: Integer Separation Lemma
content: Distinct natural numbers have absolute difference at least 1 when viewed as reals. This bridges the discrete construction (consecutive integers) with the continuous separation requirement. The proof splits on whether $a < b$ or $a > b$.

title: f₁(n) ≤ n−1: Left-Endpoint Injection
content: The key upper-bound technique: inject each unit pair into non-maximal points by mapping $(i,j)$ to whichever endpoint has the smaller coordinate. This point cannot be the global maximum (its partner is 1 unit to the right). Injectivity requires the separation property: two unit pairs sharing an endpoint must share the other endpoint too, since the left neighbor is determined by the distance constraint.

title: f₁(n) = n−1: Consecutive Integer Construction
content: The configuration $\{0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1\}$ achieves exactly $n-1$ unit pairs (each consecutive pair). The proof constructs an explicit bijection $\varphi: \text{Fin}(n-1) \to \text{unit pairs}$ mapping $k \mapsto (k, k+1)$, then shows the unit-pair set equals the image of $\varphi$.
mathContext: $f_1(n) = n - 1$, achieved by $C = \{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$ with pairs $(k, k+1)$ for $0 \le k < n-1$.

title: 1D Triangle Lemma: Rigidity of Unit Triangles
content: If $y$ and $z$ are both at unit distance from $x$ and separated from each other, then $|y-z|=2$. In 1D, two unit neighbors of the same point must be on opposite sides (one at $x-1$, one at $x+1$). This rigidity is what limits the 1D degree to 2 — a purely 1D phenomenon not present in higher dimensions.

title: 1D Degree Bound: At Most 2 Unit Neighbors
content: Three mutually separated points at unit distance from $x$ would require three points at positions $x \pm 1$, but only two such positions exist. The proof exhausts all $2^3 = 8$ sign cases for $y, z, w = x \pm 1$, showing each leads to a pair at distance 0, contradicting separation. This is the 1D incarnation of $\tau(1) = 2$.

title: Kissing Number Axioms
content: The kissing number $\tau(d)$ — maximum tangencies to a central unit sphere — is axiomatized with known values: $\tau(1)=2$ (trivial), $\tau(2)=6$ (hexagonal packing), $\tau(3)=12$ (the Newton-Gregory problem, resolved by Schütte and van der Waerden in 1953 after 200+ years). The degree bound axiom states that in any separated configuration, each point has at most $\tau(d)$ unit neighbors.

title: Handshaking Lemma (Machine-Verified)
content: The sum of all unit-distance degrees equals twice the number of unit pairs: $\sum_i \deg(i) = 2 \cdot |E|$. This is the handshaking lemma for the unit-distance graph. The proof partitions ordered pairs into $i < j$ and $j < i$ halves, shows they have equal cardinality via the swap map $(i,j) \mapsto (j,i)$ and `dist_comm`, then relates the sum of fiber cardinalities to the total. This was previously an axiom and is now fully machine-checked.
mathContext: $\sum_{i=1}^n \deg(i) = 2 \cdot \text{unitPairs}(C)$, since each edge $\{i,j\}$ contributes 1 to $\deg(i)$ and 1 to $\deg(j)$.

title: Kissing Number Bound: pairs ≤ τ(d)·n/2
content: Combines handshaking with the degree bound: $2 \cdot \text{pairs} = \sum \deg(i) \le \sum \tau(d) = \tau(d) \cdot n$. This single inequality captures the leading-order behavior of $f_d(n)$ in all dimensions. The proof chains `Finset.sum_le_sum` with `degree_le_kissing`.

title: Dimension-Specific Upper Bounds
content: Instantiating the kissing bound for dimensions 1, 2, 3: $f_1(n) \le n$ (weaker than the tight $n-1$), $f_2(n) \le 3n$, $f_3(n) \le 6n$. Each proof is a one-line substitution of $\tau(d)$. For $d=2$, Harborth's exact formula shows the true answer is $\lfloor 3n - \sqrt{12n-3}\rfloor$, so the kissing bound captures the leading coefficient exactly.
mathContext: $f_1(n) \le n$, $f_2(n) \le 3n$, $f_3(n) \le 6n$. The leading coefficients $1, 3, 6 = \tau(d)/2$ are tight.

title: FCC Cluster Lower Bound (Axiom)
content: Axiomatizes the existence of FCC lattice clusters achieving $f_3(n) \ge 6n - c \cdot n^{2/3}$. In the face-centered cubic lattice, each interior point has 12 kissing neighbors (the maximum). A ball of radius $r$ contains $\Theta(r^3)$ lattice points, of which $\Theta(r^2) = \Theta(n^{2/3})$ are on the boundary and lose contacts. This yields the $\Theta(n^{2/3})$ deficit.

title: Bezdek-Reid Upper Bound (Axiom)
content: The strongest known upper bound on unit pairs in 3D: $f_3(n) < 6n - 0.926 \cdot n^{2/3}$, proved by Bezdek and Reid (2013). Their method applies the isoperimetric inequality for finite sphere packings, bounding the surface area and hence the contact deficit. The constant $0.926$ comes from explicit computations with the isoperimetric profile.

title: The Erdős Conjecture: f₃(n) = 6n − Θ(n^{2/3})
content: The main theorem `erdos_1084_oq01` asserts that $f_3(n) = 6n - \Theta(n^{2/3})$: both constants $c_1, c_2 > 0$ exist such that $6n - c_1 n^{2/3} \le f_3(n) < 6n - c_2 n^{2/3}$. The proof is a direct conjunction of the FCC lower bound axiom and the Bezdek-Reid upper bound axiom. The mathematical content is in establishing these two bounds; the formal theorem is their synthesis.
mathContext: $\exists c_1 > 0: f_3(n) \ge 6n - c_1 n^{2/3}$ AND $\exists c_2 > 0: f_3(n) < 6n - c_2 n^{2/3}$. Together: $f_3(n) = 6n - \Theta(n^{2/3})$.

title: Isoperimetric Exponent Framework
content: Defines $\alpha(d) = (d-1)/d$ and proves its basic properties: $\alpha(2) = 1/2$, $\alpha(3) = 2/3$, $0 < \alpha(d) < 1$ for $d \ge 2$, and strict monotonicity. This unifies the 2D and 3D correction terms: Harborth's $\sqrt{n}$ correction for $d=2$ matches $n^{1/2} = n^{\alpha(2)}$, and the conjectured $n^{2/3}$ for $d=3$ matches $n^{\alpha(3)}$. The monotonicity proof uses `nlinarith` after reducing to $(d_1-1) \cdot d_2 < (d_2-1) \cdot d_1$.
mathContext: $\alpha(d) = \frac{d-1}{d}$: the isoperimetric exponent. Correction term in $f_d(n)$ is $\Theta(n^{\alpha(d)})$. Proved: $\alpha$ is strictly increasing with $0 < \alpha(d) < 1$.

title: Harborth's Formula and 2D Confirmation
content: Harborth (1974) gave the exact formula $f_2(n) = \lfloor 3n - \sqrt{12n-3} \rfloor$. The correction term $\sqrt{12n-3} \sim 2\sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{n}$ is $\Theta(n^{1/2})$, confirming the isoperimetric exponent $\alpha(2) = 1/2$. The factorization $\sqrt{12n} = 2\sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{n}$ is proved by rewriting $12n = 4 \cdot 3n$ and using $\sqrt{4} = 2$. This serves as a sanity check: the 2D case, being completely solved, validates the general framework.
